newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Nestle 1996 sales rise, sees 1997 up.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Nestle 1996 sales rise, sees 1997 up.

text.p: Nestle SA sales grew 7.1 percent to a record 60.5 billion Swiss francs ($43 billion) in 1996 as volume gains teamed up with the weakening Swiss franc to boost global turnover, the world's biggest food company said on Tuesday.

It gave an upbeat assessment for 1997 as well, forecasting sales volume would keep growing. "Barring adverse currency developments, the group should therefore register another increase in sales and profit," it said in a statement.
The statement from company headquarters in Vevey gave no profit figures for 1996, but said net profit growth should outstrip the rate at which sales increased.
"For the first time since 1993, exchange rates had a moderately positive effect of 1.4 percent," Nestle said. "Sales volume growth, excluding acquistions and disinvestments, was 2.7 percent."
It said the Asia/Pacific region, Africa and the Middle East all registered strong volume growth. Growth was above average in Europe, due primarily to rapid expansion in central and eastern Europe.

"In the Americas, Latin America achieved above-average growth, whereas the U.S. market's overall growth did not live up to expectations, particularly due to transitional problems in the beverage division," it said.
Markets welcomed the headline sales figure, which was at the higher end of expectations, and pushed Nestle registered shares up 10 francs to 1,479 before retreating a bit.
Analysts gave mostly favourable reviews, but some said Nestle should have done even better given the weakening franc.
"This is pretty positive," said Anne Alexander at Credit Suisse First Boston in London, adding it was too early to say if she would upgrade her "hold" recommendation for the stock.
"This is at the top range of the consensus, just below the 60.6 billion I was expecting."

James Amoroso at Bank Julius Baer in Zurich said the 60.5 billion figure was higher than the 60.3 billion he expected, even though volume growth was lower than his 3.1 percent forecast and the currency factor was below his 1.9 percent view.
He was perplexed at how pricing could have made up the difference because the effect of acquisitions was hardly changed from the 0.6 percent seen after 10 months.
The pricing component of growth was 2.4 percent, he said, up from 1.5 percent after 10 months.

Wilhelm Blaeuer at Pictet et Cie in Geneva said Nestle should have been able to exploit the currency factor better to wring more sales from abroad, especially as the Swiss franc started plunging in late 1996.

"I would be happy if the currency effect would be 1.7 or 1.8 percent. I don't mind this. But (it is not good) to be so low in comparison to Roche, which had 2.5 percent. We will see Novartis figures with two-point-something percent since Swiss companies have more or less the same geographically balanced portfolio."
He was referring to Swiss pharmaceutical giants Roche Holding AG Novartis AG.
Blaeuer said the difference could reflect problems Nestle acknowled it faced in the United States, where it has reorganised its coffee business to focus less on low-end market segments.
"It could show they are having real problems in the U.S.," he said. "Maybe that also has an effect on the currency side."

He said 2.7 percent volume growth was below the 3.2 percent he was expecting, adding the decline from 3.6 percent in the first half and from three percent after 10 months bode ill. He played down Nestle's forecast of rising 1997 sales and profit.
"Are they saying something which might induce anybody to upgrade their estimates? I don't think so," Blaeuer said. ($1=1.4183 Swiss Franc)
